description: We are Bio-Chem students from Isa Town Secondary School for Boys, building software to help astronauts monitor their health in space. We combine biological sciences with data analysis to protect human well-being beyond Earth. We are looking for teammates skilled in software development, UI/UX, or engineering to join us.
summary: SpaceMed is a smart medical decision-support system designed to support astronauts and crews during space missions. Instead of creating new medical hardware, the system connects to approved health information from existing astronaut monitoring equipment. It can use data such as sleep, heart rate, breathing, oxygen level, and activity. SpaceMED provides two support options. First, an astronaut can describe symptoms manually, and the AI searches a specialized medical library for possible risks, safe first steps, and escalation guidance. Second, the AI compares current health data with the astronaut’s personal baseline and identifies unusual changes, even when the astronaut does not feel symptoms. For example, a repeated decrease in sleep may indicate fatigue or stress. The system supports early action and helps medical officers make faster decisions. It does not replace doctors or provide final diagnoses. The concept is practical, scalable, and useful for future missions and remote healthcare on Earth.
details:
SpaceMED is a smart medical decision-support system designed to support astronauts during space missions. It connects approved health information from existing astronaut monitoring equipment to a specialized medical library and AI assistant.

The system has two modes. First, an astronaut can describe symptoms manually, such as dizziness, low oxygen, stress, or poor sleep. The AI searches the medical library and provides possible risks, safe first steps, and advice about when to contact the medical team. Second, the AI compares current health data with the astronaut’s personal baseline. For example, if an astronaut usually sleeps seven hours but repeatedly sleeps only five hours, the system can identify a possible risk of fatigue or stress before the astronaut notices symptoms.

The project can save time, support early action, and help astronauts and medical officers make faster decisions, especially when communication with Earth is delayed. It does not replace doctors or provide final diagnoses.

We developed the prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a responsive interface for computers, tablets, and phones. We used simulated health data to demonstrate how approved NASA data could connect to the system. No new hardware was created.

The project is creative because it combines personal health baselines, automatic risk detection, astronaut-reported symptoms, AI assistance, and a medical library in one simple system. Our team considered privacy, medical safety, false alerts, communication delays, ease of use, low cost, and human review. The intended impact is to help detect health risks earlier and support safer space missions.
